title: India demonstrates first 5.56-km free-space quantum-secure communication link
key_facts: India's Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology announced on Saturday 3 Oct 2026 the country's first free-space quantum key distribution (QKD) link, over 5.56 km.
The field trial was run by QNu Labs with BISAG-N (a government scientific society) and IIT Gandhinagar on the night of 27-28 Sep 2026, between BISAG-N and IIT Gandhinagar.
The link kept a quantum bit error rate below 5 percent and produced secure keys at 230-260 bits per second.
Keys were fed into BISAG-N's post-quantum cryptography platform Vedic Kavach to encrypt and decrypt test messages end to end.
The design combines QNu Labs' hardware QKD device Armos with software-based post-quantum cryptography and quantum random numbers, meant to stay secure if the quantum channel drops.
Free-space QKD sends keys through open air by optical link instead of fibre, a step the ministry links to future long-distance and satellite systems.
QNu Labs was founded in 2016 and builds quantum-secure communication products.
quote_evidence: According to the ministry, the trial achieved a stable Quantum Bit Error Rate of below 5 per cent and generated secure encryption keys at a rate of 230-260 bits per second.

The field trial was carried out by QNu Labs in collaboration with the Bhaskaracharya National Institute for Space Applications and Geo-informatics (BISAG-N) and IIT Gandhinagar on the night of September 27-28, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology said in a release on Saturday.
“The integration of Vedic Kavach with QNu Labs’ QKD technology marks a significant step towards practical quantum-resilient communication systems,” Dr Vinay Thakur, Director General of BISAG-N, said.
why_it_matters_hint: A government-backed open-air QKD trial is a building block for satellite-based quantum-secure networks in India.
notes: Official ministry release relayed by ANI; results are the ministry's and partners' own figures, no outside review mentioned. 5.56 km is short by international standards; the article does not compare it.
